title: SYSK Selects: Duels - A Guide to Throwing Down the Gauntlet
summary: A Stuff You Should Know Selects rerun of the 2012 episode on dueling. The hosts read and discuss Ed Grabowski's HowStuffWorks article on duels: the etymology of "duel," the role of seconds, the Irish Code Duello of 1777 and its rules (first apology, no blows, shooting in the air prohibited, no night duels), the Navy midshipman's handbook, Alexander Hamilton and Aaron Burr, dueling as a noble pastime and a way to settle debts or political rivals, trial by combat, the link to jousting and the evolution into fencing, the effect of pistols and firearms, and why dueling declined.

segments.title: Cold open and article introduction
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the Selects episode and the hosts read the opening lines of Ed Grabowski's article on how duels work. They discuss Westerns and the movie The Quick and the Dead.

segments.title: Definition and etymology of duel
segments.summary: A duel is a one-on-one battle. The word comes from Latin duellum, from duo and bellum, meaning war between two individuals.

segments.title: Throwing down the gauntlet and the role of seconds
segments.summary: A challenge was issued by throwing down a gauntlet. The second was a trusted friend who helped prepare weapons, guarded against ambush, and was supposed to try to defuse the conflict, though seconds often fought each other.

segments.title: Weapons and the Code Duello
segments.summary: Duelists typically used a heavy sword, with the same weapon for both sides, chosen by the challenger or challenged depending on the code. The Irish Code Duello of 1777 became the most widespread code, preceded by earlier German and Italian codes. Its rules aimed at injury and honor restoration rather than death, and included rules about the winner's options.

segments.title: Navy handbook and women duelists
segments.summary: The Irish code was reprinted in the U.S. Navy Midshipman's Handbook until 1862, when the Navy outlawed dueling among officers. Women rarely dueled and it was seen as an amusement. The hosts discuss Lamopen, a swordswoman, and a tangent on fighting.

segments.title: Apologies and the first-offense rule
segments.summary: Under the code, whoever gave the first offense had to make the first apology, even if the retort was worse. Striking someone was prohibited, and the alternatives were a cane, three exchanged shots, or fighting on.

segments.title: Conduct of the duel and the Hamilton-Burr duel
segments.summary: Rule thirteen prohibited shooting in the air, and duels were supposed to be wholehearted, though many participants broke this. The hosts discuss the 1804 duel in Weehawken in which Aaron Burr shot Alexander Hamilton. Night duels were generally not allowed, and seconds loaded guns in each other's presence.

segments.title: Ending a duel and dueling as noble pastime
segments.summary: Duels ended when a combatant was bloodied, disabled, or disarmed, or when a handshake was offered. Dueling distinguished nobles from commoners. Honor was tied to birth and family, and refusing a challenge meant cowardice with legal and social penalties.

segments.title: Dueling for debts, politics, and trial by combat
segments.summary: Nobles who could not work turned to dueling for entertainment and status. Duels were used to settle debts, land disputes, and political rivalries; Peter Burnett said rivals were killed off in Missouri elections between 1816 and 1824. Trial by combat served as an early legal method.

segments.title: Jousting, fencing, pistols, and decline
segments.summary: Dueling descended from medieval jousting and chivalric codes. Firearms made armor and heavy swords obsolete, leading to fencing with blunted tips. Pistols were cheaper and democratized dueling in America, though the church, military, Civil War and First World War, and spread to lower classes contributed to its decline.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close with a joke about dueling banjos and point listeners to HowStuffWorks, Twitter, Facebook, email, and the show website.
